Cecilia kicks and cries. Until her mother sets her down so Cecilia can feel with her own tiny toes the cold and crackly snow, which isn't soft and warm like she expected.  
It's the first time Cecilia learns things aren't always as they seem.

Cecilia realizes all by herself why an orchid has a petal like a bee's belly. To trick the bees, of course! They buzz over to say hello to their pretend friend, then fly off with pollen-stuffed pockets-the start of new seeds. Cecilia buzzes, too-her body humming with that lightning bolt of discovery. She wants to feel that way forever.  
Yet the fields and flowers, so full of inspiration for Cecilia, are not enough for her family.

content:
No algebra. No German. No science. Not even any friends for a shy and studious girl like her …  
yet deep inside, something glimmers and glows.  
Cecilia hides in a secret place- a dusty lab meant for older students-and studies the rows of chemicals ringing the room. Here are the pieces that put the universe together.  
At home she makes friends with her family's books on plants and Newton's laws of motion. In her heart, Cecilia crams every empty space with this kindling light. Science.

content: Miss Dalglish, a science teacher, appears in Cecilia's orbit-a new friend. She sweeps into school and blows away Cecilia's loneliness. Together they take garden walks and talk of leaves and flowers. At Christmas Miss Dalglish gives Cecilia her very own book on astronomy. Cecilia shines with joy. But Miss Dalglish grows so sick she has to leave the school.

content:
Loneliness creeps in again. But Miss Dalglish writes Cecilia letters telling her to stick to her path. And Cecilia does.  
She becomes a stellar student and wins a scholarship to study plants at the University of Cambridge. She chases new ideas like butterflies, yearning to feel that lightning bolt of discovery again.  
Yet her teachers want her to learn only the facts, to notice nothing new. Bottled up, the energy of her mind has no escape.  
But it doesn't disappear. Heat builds up deep inside. Pressure growing. Never slowing until- Cecilia hears a talk by astronomer Arthur Eddington. His work is an incandescent combination of astronomy and physics, a brand-new field to studyastrophysics! Cecilia feels the jolt, that lightning bolt again.  
And her brain buzzes with the possibility of new things just waiting to be discovered. From memory, she scribbles down every word Eddington said. Then she switches her studies to physics.  
In physics class, Cecilia is the only woman in a galaxy of men. The professor and other students tease her. Cecilia shrinks, but won't be stopped. And by graduation day she's fully formed-

content: A SCIENTIST! Ready to unlock the mysteries of the universe. So when she learns Cambridge has no place for a woman astronomer, she forms another plan: a boat ticket, a trunk filled with all her belongings, and a job in America.

content:
Cecilia blazes with that lightning bolt of understanding.  
Through her careful calculations and hours of observation, the rainbows of starlight share their secrets with Cecilia.  
They show that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, not like the rocks and minerals of our spinning planet.  
It's a stellar discovery, breathtaking- but best of all, it means other questions are rising on the horizon: If this is what stars are made of, how do they form?  
How do they create such enormous energy?  
Whose will the next discovery be?

content:
In 1925, when she was just 25 years old, Cecilia Payne discovered the exact recipe for what makes the stars. She was the first person to know. Since ancient times, men had guessed that the Earth and sun were made of the same ingredients. But how could they determine how much of each ingredient the stars contained? Cecilia found a way.  
For her thesis, she studied star rainbows, known as spectra, preserved on thousands of glass plates at Harvard. Spectra are created by passing starlight through a spectroscope, which separates light into bands of color from red to violet. You might see a similar rainbow when sunlight shines through your window at just the right angle. Each star's spectrum is cut by a series of dark lines created when atoms absorb light. By examining how light or dark the lines appeared, Cecilia was able to calculate the temperatures of different stars and determine how much of each element they contained. Her results stunned the astronomers of her time, who thought the composition of the stars was similar to that of Earth. Yet, stars are far differentmostly hydrogen and some helium, with only a sprinkling of Earth-making elements. In fact, hydrogen and helium are the most common elements in the entire universe.

metadata.Header 2: Cecilia Payne: Science Superstar 'The reward of the young scientist is the emotional thrill of being the first person in the history of the world to see something or to understand something.' -CECILIA PAYNEGAPOSCHKIN

content:
At first even Cecilia couldn't believe what she had found. But other astronomers soon arrived at the same conclusions. Cecilia's findings paved the way for astronomers to learn how stars burn bright. Today we know their power comes from slamming together hydrogen atoms, creating helium and releasing tremendous energy. Cecilia's results also laid the groundwork for much of what astronomers know about how stars are born, grow old, and die.  
As a woman working in science, Cecilia often found her path difficult. She didn't look like other scientists of her day; they were mostly men. But Cecilia proved not only what makes a star but also what makes a star scientist: curiosity, passion, hard work, and belief in oneself.

Space looks empty. But it's not. In the empty space between star systems sit …

content:
The hydrogen atoms each have the tiniest amount of gravity and are attracted to each other by that tiny amount. Yet the atoms' gravity is so weak, and the particles are so far apart, they don't pull together-yet.  
there comes a sudden jolt!  
For stars to form, astronomers think an outside force starts the hydrogen atoms moving. This could be an old star exploding or a new star forming nearby. These events send shock waves rippling through space, unsettling the cloud and moving the hydrogen atoms closer together, where gravity can do its work. Snap! Just like magnets, the hydrogen atoms start clumping up.  
Soon everything shifts and separates- As the hydrogen atoms clump together, the massive cloud splits into fragments. A single cloud can break up into thousands of smaller clouds, and each smaller cloud can form a star. This is why stars are often part of star groups or clusters.  
shrinking and smashing- The cloud fragments continue to shrink as the hydrogen atoms' gravity pulls them closer and closer together. A cloud fragment that ends up packed into a space the size of our solar system could start out 100 times bigger. Eventually the center of the cloud fragment starts to heat up as those tightly packed atoms keep energy from escaping.  
The light dims, compressed.  
yet deep inside, something glimmers and glows.

content:
The light dims, compressed.  
yet deep inside, something glimmers and glows.  
After tens of thousands of years, the center of the fragment-cloud heats up to about 10,000 kelvin, hotter than any furnace or oven on Earth. A protostar, or baby star, has formed.  
But it doesn't disappear. Heat builds up deep inside. Pressure growing. Never slowing until  
- Through the years, the protostar continues to grow hotter, and it starts to spin faster and faster as it contracts-like an ice skater who spins more quickly when they pull in their arms. The swirling gas and dust around the center flatten out, forming a disk like Saturn's rings. By this point the protostar's center can be 1 million kelvin!  
A STAR!  
Slowly, companions join the star-to-be.  
Meanwhile, planets form from the gas and dust in the disk. Just like hydrogen atoms, the gas and dust attract each other. Over time, they clump together, growing bigger and bigger and eventually forming planets. You might wonder why the gas and dust don' get pulled into the star. They are far enough away that the gravity is too weak, just like Earth is far enough from the sun to stay safely in its own orbit.  
At the center of a new solar system, the heat grows-and then, at last … a new light.  
As the protostar continues to form, it glows less brightly. That's because the protostar is compressing smaller and smaller in size. But at the same time …

metadata.Header 2: A Star Is Born In a cloud of dust and dirt, massive clouds called nebulae made of hydrogen atoms and bits of dust from dead stars.

content:
As the protostar continues to form, it glows less brightly. That's because the protostar is compressing smaller and smaller in size. But at the same time …  
the protostar keeps growing hotter, reaching 5 million kelvin. Powerful winds made of gas particles sweep its surface and blow out into space. This wind clears away any remaining gas and dust around the protostar, making it easier to see.  
Once the protostar's center reaches 10 million kelvin, the heat and pressure are so great that hydrogen atoms squish together in a process known as nuclear fusion. During fusion, the star turns hydrogen into helium and gives off lots of energy. The protostar has become a star.  
Nuclear fusion provides the heat and light we need for life on Earth. Forming a star as massive as our sun can take 50 million years or more. Once formed, such stars may live for 10 billion years before running out of hydrogen and dying out.
